5dfdfd544d96: Notice numbers two and four. The man is called Silkjær and lives at Silkjær — name and place in the same breath; the house on the cadastral plot had by then been the family’s since 1855 (Appendix A). And his neighbour needs no other address than “neighbour to Silkjær”. On this slip the place has become a fixed point that the whole row takes its bearings from.
b87effd98f2b: The man in the photograph can be named from two sources. The family’s own records give Niels Thomsen Silkjær <t1>two occupations</t1>, not one: “Smallholder & fisherman, Økjær in Husby” — and “<t2>boatman, the lifeboat station, Vedersø</t2>”. So he was not in a group picture by chance. He was a regular member of the station’s crew. [S15, S21]
2aa3413f5164: The lifeboat service’s own work of 1927 confirms his post, the date he was taken on and his length of service; there he stands with name and portrait. See the reproduction of the record below. [S58]
6e3e2463e9e6: So the picture can say what it is: around 1915 — the archive’s dating — the boatman Niels Silkjær stood in the lifeboat crew at Vedersø, 60 years old and in his thirty-seventh year at the station. Thirty-seven years earlier his father had drowned on the same coast. The father came ashore and was given a grave in Husby; Iver Kristian Olesen was the only one of the five whose body never came ashore. [S67]
445bd401061c: What made him join just then, we do not know. But the sequence stands firm and is recorded with dates in the lifeboat service’s own book: the accident in November, the appointment at New Year — at the station that had tried in vain to come to his father’s aid. Looking back, the picture is hard to miss: the sea had taken his father, and he signed up to bring other men’s fathers home. The service was not heroics; it was neighbourliness, made into a system.

65e9f7779370: <t1>The title.</t1> The book writes <t2>Baadmand</t2>, boatman — the ordinary post in the crew, not the coxswain’s. He sat at the oars and did not command the boat; the family’s word “bådsmand” covers the same post.
e30b38d008ef: <t1>The decoration.</t1> The book says he was decorated shortly after he retired — but the protocol of the Chapter of the Royal Orders shows otherwise: he was appointed on 10 November 1915, while he was still in service, recorded as “serving boatman at the Vedersø lifeboat station”. The grounds are not preserved in the Chapter’s files, but it was not a medal for bravery on one particular night — it was an honour for long and faithful service, given in his thirty-seventh year at the station. He signed the oath of loyalty at Vedersø on 30 November 1915. He wore the cross for the last twelve and a half years of his life, and it is what you see in the portrait. [S111, S112]
031210b5a153: <t1>The date.</t1> And then there is the first line, which is the one that hurts.
426c010b9811: His father drowned on 9 November 1878 and was buried on the 17th. On 1 January 1879 the son was on the lifeboat service’s payroll. Fifty-three days passed from the accident to the appointment — forty-five from the parish register’s date.
677f3ab53e66: And he did not sign up just anywhere. The newspaper wrote in 1878 that the accident happened “close to the Stage lifeboat station”, and that both the lifeboat and the rocket apparatus were brought there in vain. The station at Stage is Vedersø, as chapter 5 tells. So it was the station that could not reach his father that he joined at the turn of the year. And he stayed there until they sent him home on account of age.
c0791b8bc0bd: And then there is his own voice. Every Dannebrogsmand had to send a life account to the Chapter of the Royal Orders, and Niels Silkjær’s is still there: two handwritten pages from November 1915, together with the photograph he enclosed and the printed oath of loyalty he signed at Vedersø on 30 November. [S112]
4b7b6883daa6: His own voice · the life account of 1915
6a27f39a9e74: “I was born on 9 July 1855 in the home where I still live. As my parents were very poorly off, I had to go out into service early. From my 10th year I served with the farmers, and as soon as I was grown I went along on the fishing. At 23 years of age I married and at the same time, on my father’s death, took over my father’s home, a little property for 2 cows; but as this could not feed the family, I had still to go to work for the farmers and to the fishing when the North Sea was calm. After barely 2 years of marriage my first wife died, leaving me and a little girl. A year later I married for the second time, my wife who is still living, and in this marriage we have 10 children. I was taken on as boatman at the ‘Vedersø’ lifeboat station in 1879, the first years as a reserve and permanently employed some 4 years after, which post I still hold. It has often been very hard to provide our bread, as the day wage was small and the fishing often failed, and the pay in the lifeboat service was also small — it has now been raised over the years, which has been a good help to me that I have been glad of, and now all the children but one are grown, so now it goes tolerably well. My photograph is sent herewith. Most humbly, Niels Silkjær.”
7ffdb2ec25e4: Everything the chronicle has had to gather from scattered sources stands here in his own words: service with the farmers from the age of ten, the father’s home with two cows that could not feed the family, the first wife who died leaving him and “a little girl” after barely two years of marriage — and his father’s death and his wedding in one and the same sentence. One number sticks out: he writes ten children in the second marriage, where the parish registers know nine. The number matches the whole family of children if the daughter from the first marriage is counted — she grew up in the same household — but whether that is the conflation he made himself cannot be decided. And one piece of information is new: the 1879 appointment meant the first years as a reserve; the permanent post came only some years later. The book’s clean date covers a slower beginning.
4dd2b9474a18: The protocol in the Yellow Palace records him on page 510 — “Grounds not received by the Chapter of the Orders”, so what brought the cross just then is written nowhere. But it also records the end: a stamp about the death in June 1928, and beside it: <t1>Dek. indk. 9/7 1928</t1> — decoration received. Three weeks after his death the Cross of Honour was sent back to the Chapter of the Orders, as the rules required. The cross in the portrait was on loan — the service was his own. [S111]

6e12f4626362: The accounts do not quite add up, and that must be said. The station list divides the fifteen into six boat rescues and nine by rocket, where the book says seven and eight of him; at the “Speed” in 1885 the boat was in fact launched and worked for two hours before they gave up and saved the men by rocket, which may explain the one. 82a5764fe605: If the boat could not get out, they used the <t1>rocket apparatus</t1>: a line was shot out to the stranded ship, after which the crew hauled out a heavy hawser and made it fast round the mast, a good two feet above the tail block. Along the hawser a <t2>breeches buoy</t2> was sent out, one man at a time. The instruction board that went out with the line was printed in Danish and English. The rule was clear: women, children, passengers and helpless persons ashore first.
e19c379175bf: A station’s crew consisted of a coxswain and boatmen; the superintendent kept the records and decided when to raise the alarm. The coxswain was elected by the crew themselves and had undisputed command during rescues. The pay was a fixed yearly fee — until 1876 it was 32 kroner for a coxswain and 24 for a boatman, plus extra pay for exercises and launches. On this list Poul Bank is the superintendent, and Søren Jørgen Sørensen of Poulsgaard was a coxswain in the lifeboat service for thirty-five years. In all of Niels Silkjær’s time Vedersø had only two superintendents: Morten Th. Stage until 1908 and then Poul Pedersen Bank. Morten Th. Stage had succeeded beach bailiff Chr. M. Stage in 1864; both came from the farm the district named the station after. [S58]
c096a4b5a95f: In that order of rank Niels Silkjær was one of the boatmen — <t1>bådmand</t1>, an ordinary member of the crew, from 1879 to 1916. [S58]
4cbaee13ccd8: Vedersø was one of the original stations: the rocket apparatus came from England as early as 1851, the station was founded with the lifeboat service in 1852, and in 1854 a lifeboat built in Copenhagen arrived together with the first boathouse. On 23 November 1906 the steamship <t1>Ophelia</t1> of Helsingør stranded south of Thorsminde with a cargo of oilcake; the boats from Vedersø and Tuskjær were called out, and the Vedersø boat arrived at one o’clock. Nineteen men came ashore, by the rocket apparatus. Those are the kind of days the crew in the photograph were chosen for.
25e8206c801c: The figures say something about why it went on: in the period 1852—1925 <t1>10,500 seamen</t1> were brought ashore alive by the Danish lifeboat service. From 1914 came the first motor boats; from 1965 the boats were drawn by tractors, and in 1973 the small stations were closed.
03d5eb92c434: The lifeboat “Vedersø” was built at the naval dockyard in 1924 as the last without an engine. It turned out 38 times and was last in action in 1933, when the kuff “Farø” of Copenhagen stranded in fog with 13 men aboard — nine were saved by the boat, four by the rocket apparatus. The boat still exists; it was found in Nexø harbour and came back to Nr. Lyngvig in 2013.
